lesson_title: Scales, Directions and Slope: Reading the Country Off One Page
hook_text: Which path up the mountain is steeper: 1 to 5 or 1 to 20? Most of the class gets it backwards.
clip_script: The road atlas says 1 to 2 million. Don't panic — do one clever move: two million centimetres is twenty kilometres, so every centimetre on this page is 20 k's. Ruler on the N3: 28,5 centimetres. Times twenty — 570 kilometres. The road signs say 568. The ruler told the truth to within a suburb. Now flip inland to the Drakensberg, where the map turns to brown spaghetti. Every brown line joins ground at the SAME height, twenty metres between lines. Cross five lines? You climbed 100 metres — guaranteed. Where the lines CROWD, the mountain rears up. Now the number: gradient is climb over distance. Path one: 100 metres up over 2 000 along — 1 to 20. Path two: same 100 up, over just 500 — 1 to 5. So which is steeper? Say it as a sentence: one metre up every FIVE steps... or one metre up every TWENTY. The 1 to 5 path is the killer — smaller second number, steeper climb. Picture two ladders: 1 to 5 stands nearly upright; 1 to 20 leans back lazily. One flat page just told you how far, which way, how steep — before a single boot touched the mountain.
visual_style: A road atlas unfolding across a kitchen table, a ruler sweeping the N3 with kilometres counting up; then the map morphing into brown contour spaghetti that rises into a 3D mountain, two ladders leaning against a wall at different angles.
mood: Road-trip breezy turning summit-serious, the confidence of a navigator.
pacing: Quick win on the 570 km calculation, slow reveal as the contours rise, punchline landing on the two ladders.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read distance, direction and steepness off any map — before your legs find out the hard way.
